title: Next One by the Spot
blurb: Dagny has to pass a doctor's plumb-bob to play on, and then a fast Tanners Anchor and a coin in the wrong hand show her how much can be counted but not controlled.

blocks.text: "Next one by the spot, please," the doctor said, kindly, and the Saltpan boy beside me got up off the bench, and that made me next.

The spot was a ring of chalk on the floorboards of the Settle scale room. It was half a metre from the line of a plumb-bob that hung on a string from a hook beside the scale. My lean reaches a full metre. Half a metre is half of that.

I sat with my left hand in my father's coat pocket and counted what was hanging on that string. If it tilted toward me, the doctor would refuse me under Rule 9. I would never be registered. Match 1 would go to the Coopers, and the win we had bled for would be gone. The league would send me down to the Settle, to the lower ward Osk had never seen anybody come back from. And Rafe would carry eighty-four crowns on his own, with nobody earning a fee beside him. My throat was so tight I had to swallow twice to get a breath past it.

There were four of us on the bench that morning, first thing on the seventh day: a Lampers girl with soot under her nails, the Saltpan boy, me, and a big Tanners reserve who smelled of the lime pits and couldn't keep his knee still. Reserves for other sides. Nobody there knew me.

The doctor worked alone. He was a grey, slow man with a kind voice. He had a canvas screen at one end of the room for the bones and a desk at the other beside the scale, and he moved between them without hurrying. A long step back from the spot there was a second chalk mark on the boards, where the next one waited, out of his way.

The bench ran along the wall toward the scale. When the Saltpan boy got up, the Tanners man shuffled into his place, eager, and to keep the order I had to shuffle up too. I counted it in boot-lengths. My boots are small; four of them make a metre, near enough. I had moved up twice since I sat down, and counted both times. The end of the bench was eight boot-lengths from the line of the plumb-bob. Eight is two metres. Two metres is safe.
I looked down. The dust between the floorboards had crept out of the cracks and lay in a thin grey crescent against the toe of my left boot. I scuffed it flat with my heel.
The Lampers girl came out from behind the screen with her boots laced and her collar done up wrong.
"On the spot," the doctor said.

He didn't look at her. He had her card under his pen, and when she stepped into the chalk ring he lifted his eyes only as far as the string, and watched the plumb-bob over the top of the card. He held no watch. He watched until he was satisfied, the way my father used to watch a cable drum, and then he said, "Off," and initialled the card, and the Lampers girl went out with her registration in her hand.
"Next one behind the screen, please."

The Saltpan boy went. The screen stood half open, and from the bench I could see behind it. Boots off. Feet, both of them, in the doctor's hands. Shins, pressed with his thumbs from ankle to knee. Shirt up at the back: ribs, one side, then the other. Spine, his fingers walking down it like a man counting stair rods. Then "Dress, please," and the doctor walked back to his desk and wrote, and the boy laced his boots behind the canvas.

That was the second time I had watched it, and I counted it both times. From "Dress, please" to "On the spot" was about forty counts, because that was how long the doctor took to write up the bones. The Lampers girl had dressed in thirty-one. The Saltpan boy was taking twenty-eight.
It takes me longer than that to lace a boot. Two fingers on my left hand don't close. They were crushed in a lift-cage gate when I was twelve. I lace with my right hand and the lace end in my teeth.

The Settle lift was on the other side of that wall. I could hear its cable running on the drum. My father worked that lift every day of my childhood, and it was its cable that parted under him. My hands went cold inside my sleeves.
"Cage at the gate, Da," I said, under my breath, so low the Tanners man couldn't hear it over his own knee. "Hold the brake."
"Next one by the spot, please."

I stood. My knees didn't want to. I put my heels on the back edge of the waiting mark, as far from the string as the chalk would let me, and counted the floor. Six boot-lengths to the line. A metre and a half. My lean reaches one.
The Saltpan boy came out and stepped into the ring.
"On the spot."

I didn't breathe. If my number was wrong, the plumb-bob would lean past him toward me, and the doctor would refuse a boy who had done nothing, and then he would look up from the card, and then he would look round. I watched the string. It hung straight down.
"Off."
My number was right. A metre is a metre. It didn't make me less afraid. It only told me exactly what I was afraid of.
"Next one behind the screen, please."

His hands were cold, and I felt each place he touched as a place where something might be wrong. Feet: a week ago I had put six stone and more through those feet. Shins. Ribs: he pressed with flat fingers and I held my breath, because I didn't know what a rib feels like when the weight is still in it, and I was afraid he did. Spine. Then he lifted my left hand out of my pocket and bent the two fingers that don't bend.
"Old," he said. "Mended crooked. No bar." He put my hand back as if it were something he had borrowed. "Dress, please."
He didn't put me on the scale. The clerk's number from yesterday would stand. He walked back to his desk with my card, and I heard his pen start.
"Next one by the spot, please."
The Tanners man went; I heard his boots stop at the waiting mark. I sat on the stool behind the canvas and pulled my boots on. Right boot first. Then the left.

I will tell the truth about the left boot, because I have to tell it to somebody. I was slow because of my fingers. And then, somewhere about the second eyelet, I was slow because I had done the sum: forty counts for his pen, more than forty for my lace, and a keyed-up man standing one long step from the spot. I didn't hurry. I could have tied it badly and been out in time. I didn't.
I was three long paces from the plumb-bob, behind the canvas, with the lace in my teeth.
"On the spot," the doctor said, with my card under his pen.

The boards creaked. The Tanners man stepped into the chalk ring. Through the gap in the screen I saw his broad back and, past his shoulder, the string. It hung straight down. He wasn't leaning. He was only a stranger who wanted it over with.
I said nothing. I sat where I was and counted, because counting was the only thing keeping my hands still. Eleven. Twelve. Thirteen. Fourteen.
"Off," said the doctor. His pen scratched twice. "Next one behind the screen, please."

The Tanners man came round the canvas, red to the ears, and nodded at me as if we had been through something together. I nodded back. I took the lace out of my teeth and went out the long way, round the far side of the desk, and my card was lying on the finished pile with the doctor's initials on it. QUILLON, DAGNY. Bones: sound. Balance: sound.
"Take that to the clerk, please," the doctor said, without looking up. "Good luck today."

In the corridor my face burned and my hands wouldn't stop shaking. A stranger had stood in my place, and I had let him. He would stand on that spot again for his own card, and the doctor would read the plumb-bob twice over one honest man and never know it. It hadn't cost him a thing. It had cost me something, and I felt it go into me the way a pound of carry goes into your bones when you hold a set: no pain at first, only heavier, and staying.
I got as far as the Settle steps and sat down, because my knees wouldn't take me down them. The stone was cold through the coat.
A while later the doctor came out with his bag, done with the four of us, and stopped beside me.

"Still here, Miss Quillon? They all stare at that plumb-bob, the new ones." He said it gently. "You needn't fret. That's the last you'll see of one. There's no bob on the Lip scale, never has been. After today an Anchor only meets a plumb-bob at an inspection, and the Weighman reads those out at the Lip a match ahead. The league won't have families frightened off the plumbing."
He touched his hat and went down the steps.

He meant it as a kindness. It went into me like cold water, because it meant that one day a Weighman would stand at the Lip and read out an inspection, and there would be a whole match to wait through, and a string at the end of it, and no Tanners man to stand in my place.
Rafe was waiting at the Shaft Nine gate with his collar up.
"Registered?" he said. "Course you are. They'd have to be blind, wouldn't they?"
I held up the card, and he whooped. I didn't tell him how near it had been. Osk had said not Rafe, and I didn't want my brother carrying that too.
Osk was on the Lip in his chair, with the grit ringing its legs the way it always did. He looked at me for a long time.
"Well?"
"Registered."
He let a breath out. "One: sit down. Two: say nothing about it, not today, not to me." He paused before the word. "Three: play."
Pru was on the platform sorting the scouting chalk into its tin by colour. Dunnet leaned on the rail beside her with his big arms folded.
"What's the price on us today, Pru?" he said. "Counts reckons we'll win."

"Tanners evens," Pru said, without looking up, quick and easy. "Ninepins seven-to-four against, and that's generous. Better than last week. Last week you could have had fours on us, and the man who took fours—"
She stopped. She put a stick of blue chalk in the tin. "Price'll move by the bell," she said, flat.

The board at the Weighhouse gate had had us at two-to-one against the Coopers all that week. I had stood in front of it and read it. Fours was the price on one slip in Scarrow, and it was Rafe's, and he had shown it to me at the kitchen table with his hands flat on it. Nobody had told Pru. I filed it next to Dunnet's dropped catch, and I didn't like it there either.

At the pre-match weigh-in the Weighman read the Lip scale, wrote my weight in the book, and booked my carry as nil. He didn't blink. My bones held a stone of lean and a few pounds of the match. The book said nothing at all. From today, every number he wrote for me would be nearly two stone short of what I truly carried. It was the first lie written down about me, and I had stood on the scale and let it be written.

The Brinewell Tanners' Anchor was a narrow, quiet man called Tobin Leck, the fastest in the league. A set turns a quarter-turn every three counts for anybody; the Pin doesn't care whose hand is on it. What Leck had was that he never waited. He started his turn the moment the Cob moved, before his Caller had opened her mouth.
In Drop 1 we had the even wall. Hal held L4, and Lisbet slung me down to L6. Leck held L5, between us.

At the bell I tried to answer him, and I was always one count behind. He turned L5 toward my wall, and I turned L6 to meet it, and by the time my set came round he had turned again. Every count I chased him was a count of bodies hanging sideways in my zone, and I felt each one arrive in my ankles: a dull pressure, then a soreness that settled in to stay. Dunnet was a body-length slow off his rope on one of Pru's calls, and laughed about it after. Their Dropper rode the Cob down my own wall and into our well. Three to nothing.
I let go with the Release, breath and hand together, little finger last. Then I scuffed the chalk dust flat round my boots before Lisbet came for me.

At the Hoist the Weighman wrote my weight in the book, and the carry beside it came to a stone and two. Little more than a stone. My ankles said three. Three is the sore line, where an Anchor is slow and hurting and can still play, and I had reached it in one Drop.
"You right, Quillon?" Lisbet said, unclipping me. "You're grey."
"I'm counted," I said, and she let it be.
Hal coughed behind us, with his hand pressed flat to his side, and took it away when he saw me looking.
Osk said only one thing. "How many counts did he beat you by?"
"One," I said. "Every turn."
He nodded, slowly, and let me find the rest.

I sat on the planks and counted it again. I couldn't start faster than Leck. Nobody could. But a quarter-turn takes three counts for him the same as for me, and a half-turn takes six. If I couldn't beat him to the start, I could make him need more turn than I did.
In Drop 2 the walls swapped. I had L5 on the odd wall, with Hal on L3. Leck had L4, above me.

I set L5 before the bell, leaning down and across toward the Tanners' wall, and I held it there. When the Cob came into his zone, Leck turned the way he always turned, fast and clean. But from where I'd put my set, whatever he did, he needed a half-turn to beat it, and I needed less than a quarter to answer. His speed landed late. Dunnet took the Cob down through my zone, and I paid for the eleven counts he spent in it, and he put it in their well. Three all.
I let go with the Release. That Drop cost me under a stone, and I counted every pound of it.
The scores were level, so a coin chose the wall for Drop 3. We won the toss, and Pru kept the odd wall without asking anybody. Same ledges. Leck on L4, above me. Me on L5.

At the bell I set L5 straight across toward the Tanners' wall, flatter than in Drop 2. Leck set L4 straight across toward mine, to bring the Cob over. It fell into the Lap where his zone and mine overlap, and for a moment, as long as it takes to say it, it stopped falling. It hung there in the lamplight with nothing pulling it anywhere. Then it began to sink, very slowly, because his set and mine weren't quite opposite.
I filed it as a number: two degrees off true opposite, near enough. I didn't know yet what it was for. I only knew it was worth keeping.
Dunnet came off his rope and took the Cob as it sank. He rode it down through my zone and into the Tanners' well, roaring. Six to three.
I let go with the Release, and then I sat down in the mark, because my ankles had finished with me. By my count I held four stone and a little over.
On the Lip, the Weighman counted five crowns into each of our hands. My first match fee. I held the coins in my right fist until they were warm.
Rafe was at the rail, still shouting at the Tanners' Caller. I opened his hand, put the five crowns in it and closed his fingers over them with mine.
He went very still. "That's your fee, Dags."
"It's against the eighty-four," I said.
He looked at the coins. Then he tried to grin. "Teague'll want them polished, won't he?"

I didn't laugh. I put my hand on his arm and kept it there. My brother is sixteen and in debt to Sibbald Teague, and I love him so much that it sits in my chest like a load I'd hold for an hour if anyone would let me.
I went to sit on the bench by the Lip shed, because my ankles wouldn't keep me standing. That was how I saw it.

Behind the shed, out of the lamplight, stood the boy in the grey Tallymen scarf who runs Teague's slips at the Weighhouse gate. Dunnet was with him. The boy held out a folded note and a coin. Dunnet looked once over his shoulder, didn't see me, and took them both.

Dunnet Haig, who had named me Counts and carried the Cob down through my zone that afternoon and roared when it went in, closed his big hand over Sibbald Teague's coin and put it away like a man who had done it before.
